questions.problem: The minimum time it takes an electrician to fix a power outage is $20$ minutes, and the maximum time is $160$ minutes. Assuming that the time it takes to fix the power outage is uniformly distributed, what is the probability that a random power outage fix takes more than $30$ minutes but less than $60$ minutes?
questions.worked_solution:
Let $X$ represent the time it takes to fix a random power outage. From the problem statement, we know that $X∼U[20,160],$ and we wish to compute $P(30<X<60).$

In general, if $X∼U[a,b],$ then $X$ has the following probability density function:

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{b-a}, & a\le x\le b \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

So, for our random variable $X∼U[20,160],$ we have the following probability density function:

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{140}, & 20\le x\le 160 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(30<X<60) & ={\int }_{30}^{60}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{30}^{60}\frac{1}{140}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{x}{140}|}_{30}^{60} \\  & =\frac{60}{140}-\frac{30}{140} \\  & =\frac{3}{14}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

questions.problem: In an online poker tournament, the maximum loss is $10$ dollars, and the maximum win is $8$ dollars. Assuming that a player's earnings are uniformly distributed between $-10$ and $8,$ what is the probability that a randomly chosen player loses between $2$ and $8$ dollars?

Let $X$ represent the earnings of a randomly chosen player. From the problem statement, we know that $X∼U[-10,8],$ and we wish to compute $P(-8\le X\le -2).$

In general, if $X∼U[a,b],$ then $X$ has the following probability density function:

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{b-a}, & a\le x\le b \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

So, for our random variable $X∼U[-10,8],$ we have the following probability density function:

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{18}, & -10\le x\le 8 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-8\le X\le -2) & ={\int }_{-8}^{-2}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-8}^{-2}\frac{1}{18}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{x}{18}|}_{-8}^{-2} \\  & =-\frac{2}{18}-(-\frac{8}{18}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

In general, if $X∼U[a,b],$ then $X$ has the following expected value:

$$
\text{E}[X]=\frac{a+b}{2}
$$

So, for our random variable $X∼U[-7.5,12.5],$ we have the following expected value:

$$
\text{E}[X]=\frac{-7.5+12.5}{2}=2.5
$$

Therefore, the mean return on the investment is $2.5%.$

Let $X$ represent the duration of the radio program. From the problem statement, we know that $X \sim U[27,34],$ and we wish to compute $P(X < 30).$

In general, if $X \sim U[a,b],$ then $X$ has the following probability density function:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14214230/assets/2a615c021abbdd4009eb1debcda9b9c3076f6a9f087c6e1e6fd9454b9334eb17.svg)

So, for our random variable $X \sim U[27,34],$ we have the following probability density function:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14214230/assets/938214f94631d071b2bcd6b672e3b9b903918a88676da2cdc3b978cd94d891b2.svg)

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<30) & ={\int }_{27}^{30}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{27}^{30}\frac{1}{7}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{x}{7}|}_{27}^{30} \\  & =\frac{30}{7}-\frac{27}{7} \\  & =\frac{3}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: A museum manager notices that the minimum visiting time of visitors to the museum is $1.5$ hours, whereas the maximum time is $4.5$ hours. If the visiting time is uniformly distributed, what is its variance?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $X$ represent the visiting time of a randomly chosen visitor. From the problem statement, we know that $X \sim U[1.5,4.5],$ and we wish to compute $\textrm{Var}[X].$

In general, if $X \sim U[a,b],$ then $X$ has the following variance:

$$
\textrm{Var}[X] = \dfrac{(b-a)^2}{12}
$$

So, for our random variable $X \sim U[1.5,4.5],$ we have the following variance:

$$
\textrm{Var}[X] = \dfrac{(4.5-1.5)^2}{12} = \dfrac{9}{12} = \dfrac{3}{4}
$$

Therefore, the variance is $\dfrac{3}{4}\,\textrm{hr}^2.$

We can use a continuous uniform distribution to model situations where all possible outcomes on a finite interval are equally likely.

For instance, suppose a dental receptionist wants to model the waiting time of a randomly selected patient. After observing a number of patients over several days, the receptionist notices that the waiting time is uniformly distributed between $6$ and $14$ minutes, inclusive.

For example, the probability that a randomly selected patient waits longer than $9$ minutes is equal to

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\ge 9) & ={\int }_{9}^{14}\frac{1}{8}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{8}{\int }_{9}^{14}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{8}{[x]}_{9}^{14} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}[14-9] \\  & =\frac{5}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can also calculate the mean waiting time by finding the expected value of $X\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =\frac{a+b}{2} \\  & =\frac{6+14}{2} \\  & =10\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the mean waiting time is $10$ minutes.

tutorials.content:
In general, if $X \sim U[a,b]$ is uniformly distributed, then $X$ has the following probability density function:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14214230/assets/93894f939fa0ef715ee6ab6c225f456972b746184673df0b8d8312656727d793.svg)

We can use a continuous uniform distribution to model situations where all possible outcomes on a finite interval are equally likely.

For instance, suppose a dental receptionist wants to model the waiting time of a randomly selected patient. After observing a number of patients over several days, the receptionist notices that the waiting time is uniformly distributed between $6$ and $14$ minutes, inclusive.

Then, by letting $X$ be the amount of time a randomly selected patient spends waiting, we can model the waiting time using the continuous uniform distribution: 

$$
X \sim U[6,14]
$$

Therefore, $X$ has the following probability density function:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14214230/assets/fd37b3e19aad197ebb7eeabad00fca068455eed8da462a12630134cd7980941e.svg)

With this model, we can now make predictions about patient waiting times.

For example, the probability that a randomly selected patient waits longer than $9$ minutes is equal to

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\ge 9) & ={\int }_{9}^{14}\frac{1}{8}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{8}{\int }_{9}^{14}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{8}{[x]}_{9}^{14} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}[14-9] \\  & =\frac{5}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can also calculate the mean waiting time by finding the expected value of $X\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =\frac{a+b}{2} \\  & =\frac{6+14}{2} \\  & =10\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the mean waiting time is $10$ minutes.
